 Waiting until 70 locks in the largest monthly check Social Security offers, but the gap between men and women at that age is wider than many retirees expect.
 By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 19, 2026 at 12:03PM EST 
 + Fool.com on Share Summarize with AI Key Points
 The average monthly Social Security benefit for retirees age 70 is $2,274.68 as of December 2025. 
 Men at age 70 receive an average of $2,529.62 per month, while women receive an average of $2,024.08. 
 Delayed retirement credits stop accruing at age 70 and are worth 8% for every year you wait past your full retirement age. 
 10 stocks we like better › 
 The average Social Security benefit for someone age 70 is $2,274.68 per month, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). This age marks the end of benefit growth. You can't earn any more increases by waiting, as delayed retirement credits stop accruing once your 70th birthday arrives.
 The SSA calculates your benefit based on an average of your wages across your 35 highest-earning years. These earlier wages are adjusted for inflation. The result is processed by a formula to determine your primary insurance amount (PIA), the baseline amount you're eligible to receive at your full retirement age .
 Image source: Getty Images.
 What 70-year-olds receive
 For every year you delay claiming past full retirement age, you earn delayed retirement credits worth 8% per year. Full retirement age ranges from 66 to 67, depending on your birth year, and it's 67 for everyone born in 1960 or later. A worker whose full retirement age is 67 can earn up to a 24% increase by waiting until age 70 to claim. 
 Men who are 70 receive an average monthly benefit of $2,529.62, while the average for women is $2,024.08. That creates a gender gap of $505.54 per month, based on December 2025 data, the most recent available. These figures represent a snapshot of all retirees who are 70 today, regardless of whether they claimed early or maxed out delayed retirement credits.
 Age Overall Men Women 
 70 $2,274.68 $2,529.62 $2,024.08 
 The table above shows the average monthly benefit as of December 2025. It's important to remember that these population averages reflect thousands of individual work histories and various claiming ages. Your own check depends on your specific earnings record and the age you choose to start receiving benefits.
 Health and the long-term math
 A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027. That adjustment adds about $82 a month to the age-70 overall average. These raises are designed to help your purchasing power keep pace with inflation. However, they often fall short of fully covering the increase in senior living costs, especially in healthcare and housing.
 Social Security was only designed to replace about 40% of your pre-retirement income. Most retirees need a much higher share than that to cover their expenses, so they rely on savings or other income sources. Delaying until 70 is often a strong move for those in good health with family longevity, as it locks in the highest possible monthly check.
 Based on the data, a 65-year-old man is expected to live about 18 more years, while a woman is expected to live about 21 more years. If you live an average lifespan, you tend to receive roughly the same total amount over your lifetime regardless of when you claim. The break-even age for waiting until 70 is generally around 82 or 83.
 Delaying is also a consideration for the higher-earning spouse in a couple. Since a survivor benefit steps up to the higher earner's actual check amount, waiting until 70 can provide a lasting financial cushion for whichever spouse lives longer. Whether you beat the average depends on your work history and claiming age.
 For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide .
 Who shouldn't claim Social Security at 70?
 Claiming Social Security at 70 can be the wrong choice for those with short life expectancies. If you only live for a few more years after you sign up, you'll likely wind up with a smaller lifetime benefit than you could have gotten by claiming early. 
 Of course, no one knows exactly how long they'll live. But if this is a concern for you, you might prefer to sign up for benefits at your FRA or even earlier.
 Signing up early could also make sense if you don't have a lot of personal savings to supplement your checks and you're unable to work. You might wind up with a smaller lifetime benefit this way, but that's better than falling behind on your mortgage or rent payment or taking on debt.
